terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation; aliquid ab aliquō, or ab aliquō ut + subjunctive
evidence: Cic. Att. 1.9.2: petō abs tē ut haec dīligenter cūrēs
Cic. Fam. 9.13.3: petō igitur ā tē vel, sī pateris, ōrō ut …
terms.comment: The usual word for asking someone for something: petere aliquid ab aliquō, or petere ab aliquō ut …. Its first senses are to make for a place and to aim at, attack (Rōmam petere, caput petere); it is also to stand for office (Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation; the person in the accusative, with ut or nē + subjunctive
evidence: Cic. Fam. 13.44.1: idque ut faciās vehementer tē rogō
terms.comment: Rogō tē ut … is the commonest way of putting a request in Cicero’s letters. The same verb asks a question (rogāre aliquem aliquid; see question).

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation; aliquem ut + subjunctive
evidence: Cic. Fam. 13.66.2: etiam atque etiam tē rogō atque ōrō ut …
terms.comment: Warmer than rogō, and often paired with it. Its older senses are to speak, to plead a case, and, in Christian Latin, to pray (Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: noun, fourth declension, found only in the ablative singular
evidence: Cic. Att. 1.9.2: Thyillus tē rogat et ego ejus rogātū
terms.comment: Rogātū meō, at my request; Lewis & Short calls it Ciceronian. Seneca says it with a participle: patre meō rogante.

terms.gloss: demand, claim; ask as one’s due
terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation; aliquid ab aliquō, or ut + subjunctive
evidence: Ter. Phorm. 411: Quid est? num inīquum postulō?
terms.comment: A request made as of right, so firmer than petō: Cicero sets postulat beside poscere and flāgitāre (Lewis & Short). The thing demanded is postulātum.

phrases.latin: petō abs tē ut haec dīligenter cūrēs.
phrases.english: I ask you to see to these things carefully.

phrases.latin: hoc mihi grātius facere nihil potes, idque ut faciās vehementer tē rogō.
phrases.english: You can do nothing that would please me more, and I earnestly ask you to do it.

phrases.latin: patre itaque meō rogante … ad prīstinam cōnsuētūdinem rediī
phrases.english: so, at my father’s request, … I went back to my old habit

sources: Lewis & Short: peto · Lewis & Short: rogo · Lewis & Short: oro · Lewis & Short: rogatus · Lewis & Short: postulo
Cic. Att. 1.9.2, Fam. 9.13.3, 13.44.1, 13.66.2 and Ter. Phorm. 411 checked against the Perseus Latin texts (Purser’s sections; 11 November 2026).
